Have you ever taken a road trip in the US and thought to yourself "I wonder what La Quinta means"?
Well, the late comedian [Mitch Hedberg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mitch_Hedberg) thinks it's Spanish for *next to Denny's*.

If you're not familiar with these two establishments, [Denny's](https://www.dennys.com/) is a casual diner chain that is open 24 hours and [La Quinta Inn and Suites](http://www.lq.com/) is a hotel chain.

These two establishments tend to be clustered together, or at least this observation is a joke made famous by Mitch Hedberg.
In this lab we explore the validity of this joke and along the way learn some more data wrangling and tips for visualizing spatial data.

The inspiration for this lab comes from a blog post by John Reiser on his *new jersey geographer* blog.
You can read that analysis [here](http://njgeo.org/2014/01/30/mitch-hedberg-and-gis/).
Reiser's blog post focuses on scraping data from Denny's and La Quinta Inn and Suites websites using Python.
In this lab we focus on visualization and analysis of these data.
The data scraping was also done in R, and we will discuss web scraping using R later in the course.
For now, we focus on the data that have already been scraped and tidied for you.

# Learning goals

-   Visualising spatial data
-   Joining data frames

## Packages

We'll use the **tidyverse** package for much of the data wrangling and visualisation and the **dsbox** package for the Denny's and La Quinta datasets.

These packages are already installed for you.

```{r}
#| message: false
library(tidyverse)
library(dsbox)
```

## Data

The datasets we'll use are called `dennys` and `laquinta` from the **dsbox** package.
These data were scraped from [Denny's](https://locations.dennys.com/) and [La Quinta](https://www.lq.com/en/findandbook/hotel-listings.html), respectively.

Since the datasets are distributed with the package, they become available when we load **dsbox**.
You can find out more about the datasets by running `?dennys` and `?laquinta` in the Console or by using the Help pane in RStudio.

For this lab, we'll save shorter versions of the dataset names to use in our code:

```{r}
dn <- dennys
lq <- laquinta
```

To help with our analysis we will also use a dataset on US states, which is located in the `data` folder of your project.

```{r}
states <- read_csv("data/states.csv")
```

Each observation in this dataset represents a state, including DC.
Along with the name of the state, we have the two-letter abbreviation and the geographic area of the state in square miles.

We would like to limit our analysis to Denny's and La Quinta locations in the United States.

3.  ✏️ Take a look at the websites that the data come from, linked above.
    Are there any La Quinta locations outside of the US?
    If so, which countries?
    What about Denny's?

4.  ✏️ Now take a look at the data.
    What would be some ways of determining whether or not either establishment has any locations outside the US using just the data, rather than the websites?
    Don't worry about whether you know how to implement this yet.
    Brainstorm some ideas and write down at least one.

We will determine whether or not an establishment has a location outside the US using the `state` variable in the `dn` and `lq` datasets.
We know which states are in the US, and we have this information in the `states` data frame we loaded.

5.  ✏️ Find the Denny's locations that are outside the US, if any. To do so, filter the Denny's locations for observations where `state` is not in `states$abbreviation`. The `%in%` operator matches the states listed in the `state` variable to those listed in `states$abbreviation`. The `!` operator means **not**. Are there any Denny's locations outside the US?

> **Hint:** Filter for `state`s that are not in `states$abbreviation`.

```{r}
dn |>
  filter(!(state %in% states$abbreviation))
```

6.  Add a country variable to the Denny's dataset and set all observations equal to `"United States"`. Use `mutate()` to add the variable, and save the result as `dn` again so that the stored data frame contains the new variable going forward.

> **Note:** We don't need to tell R how many times to repeat the character string `"United States"` to fill in the data for all observations.
> R takes care of that automatically.

```{r}
dn <- dn |>
  mutate(country = "United States")
```

7.  ✏️ Find the La Quinta locations that are outside the US, and figure out which country they are in.
    This might require some searching online.
    Take notes; you will need to use this information in the next exercise.

8.  Add a country variable to the La Quinta dataset.
    Use `case_when()` to populate this variable.
    You'll need to refer to your notes from Exercise 7 about which country the non-US locations are in.

Here is some starter code to get you going:

```{r}
#| eval: false
lq <- lq |>
  mutate(country = case_when(
    state %in% state.abb     ~ "United States",
    state %in% c("ON", "BC") ~ "Canada",
    state == "ANT"           ~ "Colombia",
    ...                      # fill in the rest
  ))
```

🧶 ✅ *Complete Exercises 3–8 and render the document as both HTML and PDF. Check that your code runs without errors and that all requested written responses appear correctly in both versions.*

Going forward we will work with the data from the United States only.
All Denny's locations are in the United States, so we don't need to worry about them.
However, we do need to filter the La Quinta dataset for locations in the United States.

```{r}
lq <- lq |>
  filter(country == "United States")
```

9.  ✏️ Which states have the most and fewest Denny's locations? What about La Quinta? Is this surprising? Why or why not?

Next, let's calculate which states have the most Denny's locations *per thousand square miles*.
This requires *joining* information from the frequency tables you created with information from the `states` data frame.

First, we count how many observations are in each state, which will give us a data frame with two variables: `state` and `n`.
Then, we join this data frame with the `states` data frame.

The variable containing the two-letter abbreviations is called `abbreviation` in the `states` data frame.
When joining the two data frames, we therefore specify that the `state` variable from the Denny's data should be matched to the `abbreviation` variable from the `states` data:

```{r}
dn |>
  count(state) |>
  inner_join(states, by = c("state" = "abbreviation"))
```

Before you move on to the next question, run the code above and take a look at the output.
In the next exercise you will build on this pipeline.

10. ✏️ Which states have the most Denny's locations per thousand square miles? What about La Quinta?

Next, we put the two datasets together into a single data frame.
Before we do so, we need to add an identifier variable.
We'll call this `establishment` and set the value to `"Denny's"` and `"La Quinta"` for the `dn` and `lq` data frames, respectively.

```{r}
dn <- dn |>
  mutate(establishment = "Denny's")

lq <- lq |>
  mutate(establishment = "La Quinta")
```

Since the two data frames have the same columns, we can easily bind them with `bind_rows()`:

```{r}
dn_lq <- bind_rows(dn, lq)
```

We can plot the locations of the two establishments using a scatterplot and color the points by establishment type.

```{r}
ggplot(
  dn_lq,
  mapping = aes(
    x = longitude,
    y = latitude,
    color = establishment
  )
) +
  geom_point()
```

The following two questions ask you to create visualizations.
